meta.name: Lakeland Terrier Puppy Checklist
meta.excerpt: A Lakeland Terrier puppy is alert, energetic, and already testing limits from week one. This checklist covers supplies, socialization, and training priorities for this bold and clever working terrier.
meta.meta_description: Lakeland Terrier puppy checklist: supplies, secure yard requirements, socialization, and training tips for this bold British working terrier.

intro.label: Before Puppy Comes Home
intro.heading: Prepare for a Bold, Energetic Terrier
intro.html:
The Lakeland Terrier puppy is alert and curious from the first moment. Preparation focuses on fencing (this breed will find every weak spot), basic supplies, and finding a groomer who knows wiry terrier coats.

This guide contains affiliate links. As an Amazon Associate, Wooffy earns from qualifying purchases.

Supplies Checklist

  • Medium wire crate with divider
  • Small stainless steel food and water bowls
  • Adjustable collar and 6-foot leash
  • Front-clip harness for leash training
  • ID tag with phone number
  • Small-breed puppy food confirmed with breeder
  • Slicker brush and wide-tooth metal comb
    One option: Chris Christensen Big G Slicker Brush on Amazon. Long angled pins in a flexible cushioned pad that lift dead hair and work through leg and beard furnishings. Use light strokes; slicker pins can scratch skin if pressed hard.
  • Enzymatic cleaner for accidents
    One option: Nature's Miracle Dog Stain & Odor Remover (32 oz) on Amazon. An enzymatic stain and odor cleaner that keeps breaking down urine and other organic messes after you apply it. Spot-test on carpet or upholstery first.
  • Durable toys — terriers are vigorous chewers and players
  • Digging deterrent for fence base if needed

Yard and Home Safety

  • Inspect fencing thoroughly — the Lakeland is a digger and escape artist
  • Secure fence base with L-shaped wire along the perimeter to prevent digging out
  • Remove small animals from unsupervised access areas — the prey drive is real
  • Tuck away cords and small chewable objects

Vet and Groomer Setup

  • First wellness exam within 48–72 hours
  • Pet insurance enrolled immediately
  • Find a groomer experienced with wiry terrier coats before the puppy arrives
  • Schedule first puppy grooming intro at 10–12 weeks

care.label: First Week Setup
care.heading: Active and Ready to Learn From Day One
care.html:
The Lakeland puppy is physically and mentally alert and will be testing its environment immediately. Structure from the first day is essential.

Day 1–2

  • Crate introduction with meals inside and comfort item
  • House training schedule begins immediately
  • Begin name recognition training with high-value treats
    One option: Blue Buffalo Bits Soft Training Treats, Beef (19 oz) on Amazon. Soft, bite-size training treats with real beef as the first ingredient, small enough for rapid repetitions. Keep treats to about 10% of daily calories.

Day 3–7

  • Start harness walks — work on loose-leash walking from the very first outing
  • Positive stranger introductions with food rewards
  • Begin daily handling: feet, ears, beard area, and mouth — builds tolerance for grooming
  • Vet wellness visit
  • Book puppy obedience class

Socialization Priorities (Weeks 8–16)

  • Varied adults, children, other dogs in controlled positive settings
  • Urban sounds, different surfaces, new environments
  • Exposure to cats and small animals in controlled contexts to begin building appropriate responses
  • Building alone time — prevents separation anxiety in this people-loving breed

special.label: Training
special.heading: Consistent Training for a Smart Terrier
special.html:
The Lakeland Terrier is intelligent and responds well to positive reinforcement training. The independent streak of terrier breeds means consistency is the most important quality in a trainer — the Lakeland will exploit any inconsistency in rules.

Priority Commands

  • Sit, stay, come, leave it — the fundamentals that have real safety relevance for this prey-driven breed
  • Loose-leash walking — start immediately; terriers pull
  • Off — prevent jumping while the dog is small enough to manage easily
  • Quiet — the Lakeland's alert barking can become excessive without cues to stop

Managing Terrier Tendencies

  • Recall training requires extra investment with terriers — a Lakeland on a scent trail has selective hearing. Work recall daily in varied environments with very high-value rewards.
  • Never trust a Lakeland off-leash in an unfenced area around prey animals — the instinct is faster than training in the moment
  • Digging is natural and may be redirected to a designated digging area rather than eliminated

Building a Positive Training Relationship

  • Keep sessions short (5 minutes) and varied — the Lakeland gets bored with repetition and checks out
  • Use food rewards that the dog genuinely values — small bits of real meat often work better than kibble for terriers
  • End every session on a success so the dog looks forward to the next one

Next up: your Lakeland Terrier’s teenage months (roughly 6 months to 2 years)

  • The dog teenage phase — why a good puppy can suddenly “forget” cues, and what helps
  • How to teach a reliable recall — start before adolescence makes it harder
  • Leash reactivity — what to do if barking or lunging on leash starts
  • When to spay or neuter — the best age depends on size and breed

faq.a: All puppies bite during teething and play — terrier puppies often bite with particular enthusiasm. Redirect to appropriate chew toys, calmly say 'ouch' and withdraw attention, and be consistent. Bite inhibition training should begin the first day home.

faq.q: Can a Lakeland Terrier live with cats?
faq.a: With careful introduction and supervision, some Lakelands coexist with cats they have been raised with. However, the strong prey drive means interactions should always be supervised and introductions done extremely gradually. Lakeland Terriers should never be trusted with small pets like rabbits, hamsters, or guinea pigs.

faq.q: How do I prevent my Lakeland Terrier puppy from digging?
faq.a: Digging is hardwired in terriers and cannot be completely eliminated. Secure fence lines with buried mesh or L-shaped wire to prevent escape. Consider designating a legal digging area (a sandbox or soft garden bed) where digging is permitted and rewarded — redirection works better than prohibition for terrier instincts.
